 Food-Assistance Restrictions Can Curb Soda Purchases 
 Bans on purchases of soda and other sweetened drinks reduce consumption.
By 
 Katia Savchuk 
November 19, 2026 
 CBR - Public Policy 
 Share This Page 
 Share This Page --> 
 In May 2025, the US Department of Agriculture began granting waivers allowing states to ban the use of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits to buy soda and other sugary drinks. Many policymakers quickly embraced the idea. “It is a tremendous step toward improving the health and well-being of our state,” said Nebraska governor Jim Pillen, whose state received the first such waiver. Since then, 22 states have followed suit. 
 Pillen’s forecast about better health outcomes was not obvious. “Standard economic theory predicts that removing sugary drinks from SNAP will not affect purchases,” write Stanford’s Hunt Allcott  and Anna Grummon , MIT’s Amy Finkelstein , and Chicago Booth’s Matthew J. Notowidigdo . 
 But the research team finds that the policy did in fact make progress toward that goal. They looked at consumer behavior in the first 10 states to implement restrictions, with bans that went into effect between January and April 2026, and find that purchases of sugary drinks by households receiving food stamps fell by more than 12 percent in the first half of 2026. The researchers estimate that expanding the ban nationwide would yield $1.1 billion in economic benefits, mostly by reducing healthcare costs. 
 Created in 1964, SNAP, also called food stamps, provides food subsidies to about 42 million US residents; participants receive about $188 a month on average. Past research has shown that sugary beverages, such as soda and energy drinks—which have been linked to health problems such as obesity and type 2 diabetes—account for 9 percent of SNAP spending. 
 Debates over whether to curtail recipients’ ability to spend on sweetened drinks go back decades. But not until 2025, amid President Trump’s embrace of the Make America Healthy Again movement, did the federal government start approving states’ requests to do so. 
 Many experts have been skeptical of such restrictions. When Allcott, Finkelstein, Grummon, and Notowidigdo surveyed 336 economists and public-health researchers as part of their study, nearly 30 percent predicted there would be no effect on purchases, while about half expected consumption to fall by 5 percent or less. 
 The researchers analyzed data housed at Chicago Booth’s Kilts Center for Marketing on grocery purchases from about15,000 households receiving SNAP benefits across the country. The data, provided by market-research firm Numerator and supplemented by information from NielsenIQ, noted whether each item was bought with food stamps. Between January and June 2026, SNAP recipients in states where bans went into effect reduced purchases of sugary drinks by 404 fluid ounces—the equivalent of 34 12-ounce cans. Households that relied on foods stamps for a larger share of their grocery bill were more likely to significantly reduce purchases of banned drinks, the study finds.
 In states that only banned certain sugary drinks—such as soda but not sports drinks—SNAP recipients offset up to 39 percent of the reduction in calories from restricted items by buying more of the allowed sweetened beverages. “Since sugary drink categories are moderately substitutable, continuing to include some sugary drinks in SNAP will naturally undo some of the potential consumption reductions,” the researchers write. 
 Less sugar in the shopping cart
 SNAP households purchased about 12 percent fewer restricted drinks after bans in their states took effect. Overall, purchases of sugary drinks dropped even though households could still opt to pay for them outside their SNAP budget.
 Households didn’t seem to cut back because the government was sending a signal that it thinks sugary drinks are unhealthy. As part of their study, the researchers surveyed 9,000 people whose spending data were captured by Numerator, about half of whom reported receiving food stamps. Participants answered questions in December 2025, before restrictions went into effect, and seven months later. Bans didn’t significantly affect recipients’ perceptions of the health risks of sugary drinks, the researchers find. Instead, they write, lower consumption was consistent with other research demonstrating that SNAP recipients tend not to treat food stamps as interchangeable with cash. 
 While the researchers argue that a nationwide sugary drink ban would produce health benefits and reduce government spending, they also find evidence that the policy has negative consequences. The surveys made clear that the bans increased respondents’ feelings of being judged when using food stamps and their perceptions that food-stamp policies in their state “are disrespectful” or “take away personal freedom.” 
 The fate of such bans is unclear. In June 2026, a federal district court blocked five states—including Nebraska—from moving forward with restrictions on using food stamps to buy sugary drinks and foods, ruling that the Department of Agriculture lacked the authority to approve their requests. And the policy is unpopular among those who use SNAP: Only 18 percent of recipients say they “strongly support” the restrictions, compared with 34 percent of people who don’t receive food stamps, the researchers find.
 Works Cited
 Hunt Allcott, Amy Finkelstein, Anna Grummon, and Matthew J. Notowidigdo, “The Effects of SNAP Sugary Drink Restrictions on Consumption and Welfare,” NBER working paper, August 2026.
